{"input": {"strat_id": "RHAISTRAT-8004", "strategy_title": "Default Vector Store for Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag", "strategy_markdown": "## Summary

RHOAI must provide a default vector store that is available out-of-the-box — without manual setup — so that Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag continue to function when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution image. Today these capabilities depend on an inline vector store provider bundled within the Llama Stack process; removing it (per RHAISTRAT-7474) will break them unless an alternative is available at the platform level.

## Problem Statement

Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag currently rely on an inline Milvus provider embedded in the Llama Stack distribution image to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This inline provider runs inside the Llama Stack process itself.

RHAISTRAT-7474 proposes removing inline providers from the Llama Stack distribution to improve GA readiness — shipping only what can be tested and maintained at scale, and aligning with Llama Stack's primary use case as a remote API server. However, no platform-level alternative exists today. If inline providers are removed without a replacement, any RHOAI user relying on Gen AI Studio's RAG capabilities or Auto Rag will lose functionality entirely — there is no workaround short of manually provisioning and configuring an external vector database.

Users expect vector storage to "just work" when they use Gen AI Studio or Auto Rag. The current out-of-the-box experience must be preserved even as the underlying architecture evolves.

## Affected Customers

* All RHOAI customers using Gen AI Studio playground with RAG capabilities
* All RHOAI customers using Auto Rag
* This is a platform-level product dependency: these features cannot function without a vector store

## Business Justification

* **Product integrity:** Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag are GA-track capabilities in RHOAI. Removing the inline vector store without a replacement breaks shipped product functionality for every user of these features.
* **Blocking dependency:** RHAISTRAT-7474 (removing inline providers for GA readiness) cannot proceed until this RFE is resolved. Silas Brenmark (Gen AI Studio lead) has identified this as a blocker.
* **User experience:** RHOAI differentiates on integrated, opinionated defaults. Requiring users to manually provision and configure a vector database before they can use the playground or Auto Rag degrades the out-of-the-box experience that customers expect from the platform.

## Acceptance Criteria

* \[ \] A default vector store is available out-of-the-box on RHOAI without requiring users to manually provision or configure external infrastructure
* \[ \] Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] Auto Rag functions with the default vector store with no loss of current capability
* \[ \] The default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the Llama Stack instance (not an inline provider)
* \[ \] The default vector store is scoped appropriately for multi-tenant environments (e.g., per-namespace isolation)
* \[ \] The default vector store is lightweight enough to run in resource-constrained environments without imposing significant overhead

## Success Criteria

* Users of Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag experience no functional regression when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution
* No additional manual setup steps are required for RAG workflows compared to the current experience
* RHAISTRAT-7474 is unblocked and can proceed to implementation

## Open Questions

* What is the preferred scoping model — per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both? (Silas noted per-namespace is preferred for isolation, but Auto Rag may need per-instance scoping)
* Should users have a migration path from the default vector store to a production-grade vector database? (Bram Sundqvist raised the importance of aligning with commonly-used vector DB providers for easier migration)

## Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)

> **Note:** The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: `RHAISTRAT-8004-strategy.md`.

## Staff Engineer Input

**Correction 1 — OGX does not auto-provision PostgreSQL.** OGX defaults to SQLite for storage (`storage.kv.type: sqlite`, `storage.sql.type: sqlite` in the OGXServer CRD). The odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF hardcodes SQLite when creating OGXServer instances for the playground (`kv_sqlite` and `sql_sqlite` in `llamastack_config.go`). PostgreSQL is a supported backend but must be user-configured with an explicit `connectionString` secret. The strategy's claim that "every LlamaStackDistribution instance requires a PostgreSQL database" is incorrect — introducing PostgreSQL is new work, not an extension of existing infrastructure.

**Correction 2 — A Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector already exists.** The `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` image includes pgvector out of the box — confirmed in the [sclorg/postgresql-container Dockerfile](https://github.com/sclorg/postgresql-container/blob/master/16/Dockerfile.rhel9) (`INSTALL_PKGS="$INSTALL_PKGS pgvector"`). PostgreSQL 18 (RHEL 9) also includes pgvector. Furthermore, the model-registry-operator already uses `postgresql-16` as its auto-provisioned database image, and `RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected installs. No custom image build is needed. No Konflux onboarding is needed. The 1-2 sprint image onboarding estimate in the strategy can be eliminated.

**Architectural direction — platform-level database vs. self-provisioned.** Multiple RHOAI components now need PostgreSQL (model-registry, MLflow, and now OGX for pgvector). The preferred long-term direction is a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL managed via the DSC, where each component consumes a connection string rather than self-provisioning. A shared platform-provided PostgreSQL via DSC will not be available until RHOAI 3.6. For 3.5, Gen AI Studio must provision its own PostgreSQL instance.

**Operator dependency for self-provisioning (RHAISTRAT-7164).** Self-provisioning PostgreSQL following the model-registry-operator pattern requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio. The ogx-k8s-operator is upstream and cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic. The dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) would provide this operator layer. This is a hard dependency — until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live. It will be challenging to commit this strategy to a specific release until that dependency is delivered.

**Fallback if RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time.** If the dashboard modularization is not ready for 3.5, the fallback is to require customers to bring their own PostgreSQL for RAG capabilities in the Playground. Users would manually configure the OGXServer CR spec with their PostgreSQL connection details. This aligns with the breaking changes introduced in OGX 1.0, even though the Playground largely abstracts OGX from users. The development team should define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning.

**Decouple from Auto Rag.** Auto Rag integration with Gen AI Studio (RHAISTRAT-7824) is targeting RHOAI 3.6. This strategy should validate pgvector only for Gen AI Studio Playground RAG workflows. Auto Rag compatibility with pgvector will be addressed in RHAISTRAT-7824's scope. Remove Auto Rag from affected components, impacted teams, acceptance criteria, and validation requirements.

**Performance and index thresholds — dev experimentation scope.** The default pgvector instance is meant for development experimentation, not production usage. Strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99) are not required. The sprint 1 benchmark should capture the inline Milvus baseline and verify pgvector is in the same order of magnitude, not meet a specific threshold. Typical Playground RAG usage involves small document sets — flat scan (no index) is sufficient for the default. Users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database. Remove open questions about latency thresholds, corpus size ranges, and index type selection.

**PostgreSQL resource sizing.** Reference the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits as the starting point. Adjust based on sprint 1 benchmarking if needed.

**Alternative fallback — BFF-managed PostgreSQL provisioning.** If RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time, an alternative to requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL is to have the gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly, similar to how the BFF currently provisions guardrails infrastructure. The BFF would create the PostgreSQL Deployment, Service, PVC, and Secret when a playground with RAG is configured, if one does not already exist in the namespace. Caveats: (1) the implementation must be designed for portability — when the platform-provided shared database becomes available (3.6), the BFF should consume the shared connection string rather than self-provisioning; (2) lifecycle management of the PostgreSQL instance must be carefully considered — the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation need explicit design attention.

**Existing remote vector store implementation is reusable.** Per the engineering team, the existing remote vector store implementation can be largely reused for pgvector integration. The majority of the work effort is around infrastructure and provisioning of the PostgreSQL/pgvector database, not the vector_io provider integration itself.

**Correction 3 — Vector storage and application storage are independent configurations.** The OGX vector_io provider configuration (`remote::pgvector` via `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`) is completely separate from OGX's application storage backend configuration (`storage.kv.type`, `storage.sql.type`). This strategy only needs to configure the pgvector vector_io provider — it does not change the application storage backend, which remains on its existing default (SQLite). There is no SQLite-to-PostgreSQL migration concern because the application storage is not being touched. Remove any references to consolidating vector and application storage in a single database, and remove any SQLite-to-PostgreSQL upgrade path considerations.

# Go/no-go decision: operator availability and PostgreSQL provisioning approach

## Description

This investigation resolves the central uncertainty of the strategy: whether the dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) will deliver the RHOAI-controlled operator layer in time for the target release, and therefore which PostgreSQL/pgvector provisioning approach the default vector store uses — operator-based self-provisioning (following the model-registry-operator pattern) or gen-ai BFF-managed provisioning (the fallback). The Staff Engineer Input identifies this as a hard dependency: until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live, and the development team should define a go/no-go gate as part of sprint planning.

## Scope

- Define the go/no-go criteria and decision date for the RHAISTRAT-7164 dependency (what "delivered in time" means for the target release).
- Assess RHAISTRAT-7164 delivery status and trajectory against those criteria.
- Select the provisioning approach for the default pgvector instance: operator-based self-provisioning versus BFF-managed provisioning.
- Record the contingency if neither approach is viable for the release (customers bring their own PostgreSQL, configuring the OGXServer CR spec with their connection details).
- Confirm the scoping model for the default vector store (per-namespace isolation preferred; the operator path follows the model-registry-operator per-instance pattern).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A decision record is published that names the selected provisioning approach and the evidence used to select it.
- The go/no-go criteria and decision date for the RHAISTRAT-7164 dependency are documented in the decision record.
- The contingency path (bring-your-own PostgreSQL) and its user-facing implications are documented in the decision record.
- The scoping model (per-namespace vs per-instance) is stated in the decision record.

## HLR Traceability

- Enables AC-1 (default vector store available out-of-the-box) by selecting the provisioning approach that delivers it.
- Resolves the strategy's open question on the preferred scoping model (per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both).
- Addresses the Staff Engineer Input's requirement for a sprint-planning go/no-go gate on the RHAISTRAT-7164 dependency.

# Configure pgvector vector_io provider for Gen AI Studio playground OGX servers

## Description

This epic configures the Gen AI Studio playground's OGX server instances to use the remote pgvector vector_io provider as their default vector store, so playground RAG workflows keep functioning when inline providers are removed from the OGX distribution. The OGX distribution's existing remote vector store implementation is largely reusable — the work is configuration wiring in the gen-ai BFF, not provider development.

## Scope

- In the odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF, where OGXServer instances are created for the playground, set the vector_io provider configuration to the remote pgvector provider (`remote::pgvector`, enabled via `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`), alongside the existing storage configuration logic.
- Wire the PostgreSQL connection details (connection string / credentials secret) into the OGXServer configuration, consuming whichever connection string the selected provisioning approach provides.
- Leave the OGX application storage backend untouched (it remains on its existing SQLite default) — vector storage and application storage are independent configurations.
- Document the limitation that the default vector store targets development experimentation; users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database.
- If the OGXServer CR spec cannot carry the vector_io provider configuration, coordinate the required ogx-k8s-operator passthrough change (see Risks).

## Acceptance Criteria

If the lower-priority HLR is incidental to the P0 work (error handling, doc coverage, config override that falls out of the same implementation) or is tightly coupled to the same implementation surface, keep it bundled — splitting tightly coupled work creates duplication and artificial boundaries.\n99\t- **Redundant / overlapping HLRs — consolidate, never split:** strategies merged from multiple sources sometimes state one capability twice in different words (e.g. \"select two or more runs and view their parameters and metrics side by side\" and \"a diff view highlighting which parameters and metrics changed between two selected runs\" — the diff view is a presentation mode of the same comparison surface over the same run data). When two HLRs describe the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint for the same component and team — one a restatement or presentation mode of the other — they are ONE capability: cover both with a single epic whose HLR Traceability lists both HLR ids, at the higher of the two priorities. Do not split them into separate epics by priority label: on a shared surface a P0/P1 pair is redundant wording, not a deferral signal, and splitting produces two epics building the same surface plus an artificial serialization edge between them — a boundary violation even when the second epic only extends the first's surface.\n100\t- `docs-authoring` priority exception: `docs-authoring` epics are exempt from priority inheritance. They do not push their priority upstream to the implementations they depend on. Instead, derive their priority from the strategy frontmatter `priority` field: Critical→P0, Major→P1, Normal/Minor/Undefined→P2. If the field is missing or empty, default to P2.\n101\t\n102\t## Step 5: Build Dependency DAG\n103\t\n104\tApply these rules to construct edges between epics:\n105\t\n106\t### Epic Boundary Rules\n107\t1. Different component OR different team → separate epics\n108\t2. Same component + same team + same logical change → single epic. When splitting within a single component, split along two axes:\n109\t   - **Architectural sub-system boundaries**: backend API vs. frontend plugin, Go service vs. React UI, etc.\n110\t   - **Work-product type boundaries**: code implementation, content authoring (sample notebooks, tutorials, curated examples), and documentation are different kinds of work — they require different skills, different review criteria, and produce different PR review cycles. An epic that mixes code implementation with content authoring should be split even if the same team owns both. **Exception — incidental documentation touch-ups:** updating captions, screenshots, or references that fall out of a code change (no new content authored) is not a separate work stream — fold it into the originating epic as scope/acceptance criteria rather than a standalone `docs-authoring` epic. Only substantive content/documentation authoring (new tutorials, sample notebooks, curated examples, new or rewritten doc topics), or a strategy with `Documentation Support: Yes`, warrants a separate epic.\n111\t   These axes take precedence when deciding where to draw epic boundaries within a component. Step 4 may additionally split by priority when features are genuinely deferrable — but the initial boundary structure should come from architecture and work-product type, not from walking down the HLR list. Never split such that two epics must build the same data structure, UI surface, or API endpoint independently.\n112\t\n113\t### Investigation Edges\n114\t3. Investigation determines scope/existence of downstream work → blocking edge to all affected Implementations. Every downstream epic gated by an Investigation is a true gate (`remove` if the epic may not exist, `rewrite` if scope/approach changes, `add_remediation` if the investigation may reveal a problem requiring additional work) — record this in Step 8b when writing frontmatter. Bounded outcomes (≤3): conditional branches. Unbounded: phased decomposition.\n115\t4. Investigation is informational only (doesn't change what gets built) → not a true Investigation. Reclassify as an acceptance criterion on the relevant Implementation epic, or as an Implementation that produces a deliverable.\n116\t\n117\t### Implementation Type Ordering\n118\t5. `repo-onboarding` → `konflux-onboarding` always serial (pipeline needs repo)\n119\t6. `repo-onboarding` → general implementation of onboarded component always serial (code needs repo). Doesn't block other repos.\n120\t7. `license-validation` ∥ `repo-onboarding` parallel (independent inputs)\n121\t8. `license-validation` ∥ `konflux-onboarding` parallel (config doesn't depend on specific deps)\n122\t9. `license-validation` → general implementation serial (if licenses fail, deps change, affects approach)\n123\t10. `konflux-onboarding` ∥ general implementation parallel (config independent of code; AC gates first execution). **Add NO blocking edge in either direction.** It is tempting to make the general implementation depend on `konflux-onboarding` (\"the code needs a build pipeline first\") — do not. That coupling is enforced by the Rule 25 \"build pipeline green\" AC on the general implementation epic, never by a DAG dependency. A `konflux-onboarding → general` edge serializes work that must run in parallel and is a rule violation. This holds for EVERY `konflux-onboarding` × general-implementation pair in the decomposition, whatever the general epic's component or deliverable — a stack-wide assembly, packaging, or evidence epic that consumes the pipeline's outputs is still a general implementation. There is no \"different component\" or \"genuine artifact dependency\" exemption: if the coupling is real, express it as an AC on the consuming epic (\"the signed attestations from the build pipeline are included and validated\"), never as an edge.\n124\t11. `docs-authoring` blocked by ALL Implementation epics in strategy (always last; docs describe what was built). These edges do not trigger priority inheritance — see Step 4 `docs-authoring` priority exception.\n125\t\n126\t### Implementation → Implementation Edges\n127\t12. Framework/library → consumer Implementations always serial (consumers build against framework)\n128\t13. Implementation producing artifact another epic's code builds against (API, CRD, library) → consuming Implementation serial. Does NOT apply to configuration references (image digests, endpoint URLs) — those are AC gates. **In particular, an image digest / SHA consumed by OLM/CSV packaging (`RELATED_IMAGE`) is a configuration reference, not a build-against artifact: the packaging epic gets a \"pinned image digest available\" AC, NOT a `dependencies` edge on the image-build or `konflux-onboarding` epic.** Wiring such an edge both mis-serializes parallel work and violates Rule 10 — the digest is filled in at execution time, so the epics run in parallel. The same holds for any build-pipeline output another epic consumes as CONTENT — signed attestations, SBOMs, provenance, scan results: the consuming epic gets an AC (\"the evidence package includes the signed attestations produced by the build pipeline\"), not an edge. Code builds against an API, CRD, or library; it does not build against attestations or digests.\n129\t14. Implementations in different repos, no shared artifacts → parallel\n130\t15. Implementations in same repo, different areas → parallel (merge conflicts = coordination risk, not dependency)\n131\t\n132\t### External Dependency Edges\n133\t16. External dependency Implementation (upstream PR/RFC) → Tier 2 Implementations always serial (gated by acceptance)\n134\t17. External dependency Implementation ∥ Tier 1 Implementations always parallel (Tier 1 delivers independent partial value)\n135\t18. External dependency with uncertain timing → always evaluate for tiered delivery (see Step 5.5)\n136\t\n137\t### Epic Generation Rules\n138\t19. Safety-critical strategy (guardrails, sandboxing, RBAC) → generate fail-mode Investigation + security Investigation, both blocking main Implementation\n139\t20. New component not in architecture context → generate onboarding chain: `repo-onboarding` + `license-validation` (parallel start) → `konflux-onboarding` (after repo-onboarding) → general implementation (after license-validation; parallel with konflux-onboarding). For new container image in existing repo: skip repo-onboarding, start with image build Implementation + `konflux-onboarding` (parallel).\n140\t21. External community dependency where team submits PR/RFC and acceptance gates downstream → generate upstream Implementation epic, evaluate tiered delivery. If viable fallback exists (cherry-pick, fork) → note as AC, not separate epic. If third party resolves → model as precondition with tiered delivery, no separate epic.\n141\t22. Infrastructure not in platform inventory → generate validation Investigation (does it exist/work?) + provisioning Implementation\n142\t\n143\t### Acceptance Criteria Rules\n144\t23. Strategy replaces existing capability → add rollback/feature-flag AC to replacing Implementation epic\n145\t24. `docs-authoring` epic → add \"technically reviewed against implementation\" AC\n146\t25. Implementation with `konflux-onboarding` in dependency chain → add \"build pipeline green\" AC\n147\t\n148\t## Step 5.5: Detect Tiered Delivery\n149\t\n150\tWhen an external dependency has uncertain timing:\n151\t\n152\t1. Can the strategy deliver partial value without it?\n153\t2. **YES** → Split into:\n154\t   - **Tier 1**: Independent work (user-facing features OR risk-reduction spikes/validations)\n155\t   - **Tier 2**: Dependency-gated work (blocked by upstream epic)\n156\t3. **NO** → Linear dependencies; external dependency blocks all downstream\n157\t\n158\t## Step 6: Classify Epics\n159\t\n160\tFor each epic, determine:\n161\t\n162\t### Type (mandatory)\n163\t- **Implementation**: Produce an artifact (code, config, docs, manifests, pipelines, RFCs, upstream PRs)\n164\t- **Investigation**: Resolve uncertainty (answer a question or make a decision that other epics depend on)\n165\t\n166\t### Implementation Type (optional routing label)\n167\t\n168\t| Label | When to apply |\n169\t|-------|--------------|\n170\t| `docs-authoring` | Red Hat docs content process — specialized tooling |\n171\t| `konflux-onboarding` | Build pipeline onboarding — known-recipe |\n172\t| `license-validation` | License scanning for transitive dependencies |\n173\t| `repo-onboarding` | Midstream repo fork creation under opendatahub-io |\n174\t| _(absent/null)_ | General-purpose — read target repo, figure it out |\n175\t\n176\t### AI Implementability Signals\n177\t\n178\tScore signals so the pipeline can compute an AI-implementability classification deterministically. **Do not compute the total score or classification yourself.** Use the signal set that matches the epic `type` — Implementation and Investigation epics measure different things.\n179\t\n180\t#### Implementation epics → `ai_signals` (9 signals)\n181\t\n182\tEvaluate each as +1 (favorable), 0 (neutral/N/A), or -1 (unfavorable). Write the values into `ai_signals`.\n183\t\n184\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | +1 Condition | -1 Condition |\n185\t|---|--------|----------------|-------------|-------------|\n186\t| 1 | Change specificity | `change_specificity` | Exact file paths, API endpoints, field names known | Vague scope (\"improve X\") |\n187\t| 2 | Pattern precedent | `pattern_precedent` | Similar changes exist in same codebase | No precedent in codebase |\n188\t| 3 | Adapter/plugin pattern | `adapter_pattern` | Follows existing reference implementation | N/A (0 if absent) |\n189\t| 4 | Existing foundation | `existing_foundation` | Extending existing code/feature | Greenfield, no foundation |\n190\t| 5 | Open questions | `open_questions` | All design decisions resolved for this epic | Open questions that would change implementation approach |\n191\t| 6 | External dependency | `external_dependency` | None | Upstream contribution or vendor coordination needed |\n192\t| 7 | Human process gates | `human_process_gates` | None | Requires human approval step |\n193\t| 8 | Repo access | `repo_access` | AI can clone and modify target repo | Repo inaccessible or special access required |\n194\t| 9 | Architecture claims | `architecture_claims` | Epic's scope or the strategy's premise about the component (surfaces, repos, deployment model, maturity state such as Tech Preview/GA) is corroborated by an architecture-context file — name that file in the rationale | Strategy asserts architecture that the context files contradict or cannot back |\n195\t\n196\t**Scoring `architecture_claims` (signal 9):** a strategy makes architecture claims whenever it states what a component IS — its maturity state (\"shipped as Tech Preview\", \"generally available\"), its CRD/API/repo surfaces, its deployment model — even when it never uses the word \"claim\". A strategy premise that drives the decomposition (e.g. a maturity gap motivating a hardening program) is an architecture claim. Check `.context/architecture-context/` for the epic's components: score +1 when a context file corroborates the premise or grounds the epic's scope, and cite that file in the rationale; score -1 when the strategy asserts something the context contradicts; score 0 only when no context file covers any component the epic touches. \"The strategy makes no specific architecture claims\" is not a valid 0 rationale when context files exist for the components in scope.\n197\t\n198\t#### Investigation epics → `investigation_signals` (5 signals)\n199\t\n200\t**Do not use the 9 Implementation signals for Investigation epics.** Those penalize the *defining* traits of an investigation (open questions, no prior foundation, external dependency), so they mis-route nearly every investigation to Low — even ones the AI resolves easily. Instead score these five, which predict whether the AI investigation skill can resolve the unknowns (→ assign to the skill) or a person must (→ assign to a person). Write the values into `investigation_signals`.\n201\t\n202\t| # | Signal | Frontmatter key | Range | How to score |\n203\t|---|--------|-----------------|-------|--------------|\n204\t| 1 | Question specificity | `question_specificity` | -1 / 0 / +1 | +1 concrete, enumerable questions with a defined pass/fail criterion; -1 vague or criterion undefined (a human must frame it first) |\n205\t| 2 | Source accessibility | `source_accessibility` | 0 / +1 | +1 a readable artifact that **contains or determines the answer** exists (open repo, docs, public record). 0 when the only readable material does **not** hold the answer — e.g. a decision/PR still under review (the answer doesn't exist yet) |\n206\t| 3 | Local runnability | `local_runnability` | 0 / +1 | +1 the components can be exercised as a downloaded **binary or pip/npm library** locally — including backing a datastore with an embedded/bundled server (e.g. `pgserver` for PostgreSQL). 0 only if it genuinely can't run without a container/cluster |\n207\t| 4 | Cluster/hardware dependence | `cluster_hardware_dependence` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 some *peripheral* questions need a live cluster / GPU / prod-scale. -2 a *gating* question does. **What an operator/controller _generates_** (rendered CR, template, NetworkPolicy, RBAC in its source repo) is readable source — score it under `source_accessibility`, **not** here; only the *as-deployed runtime state* of a live cluster counts as a dependence |\n208\t| 5 | Human judgment required | `human_judgment_required` | -2 / -1 / 0 | 0 none. -1 a *peripheral* question needs a stakeholder/product decision or external-party input. -2 the *gating* question is itself a human/governance decision or external coordination the AI cannot make (e.g. \"is this ADR approved?\") |\n209\t\n210\tThe pipeline routes: **High** → assign to the investigation skill; **Medium** → hybrid (skill resolves the desk/local parts and hands a spec to a human for the rest); **Low** → assign to a person.\n211\t\n212\tWrite the signal rationale to a separate file `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN-ai-signals.md` (one per epic), for whichever signal set you used. Format as a markdown table with Signal, Value, and Rationale columns. Do not write the signals table into the epic body.\n213\t\n214\t## Step 6.5: Health Warnings\n215\t\n216\t### Non-blocking warnings (decomposition proceeds, human verifies later)\n217\t- Priority inversions (P0/P1/P2 inconsistent with technical complexity/reliability)\n218\t- Scope traps: ACs implying infrastructure that doesn't exist, contradictions between out-of-scope items and NFRs, storage beyond design intent\n219\t\n220\t### Handling unclear strategy passages\n221\t\n222\tWhen the strategy is unclear about something, apply this two-way distinction:\n223\t\n224\t| Situation | Handling |\n225\t|-----------|---------|\n226\t| **Implementation detail** — the team will resolve this when they start the work (version choices, API surface discovery, config decisions, validation of assumptions) | Not a flag. Capture as an AC on the relevant epic if needed. Most unclear passages fall here. |\n227\t| **Genuine unknown** — nobody knows yet, resolution requires technical work, and the answer changes which downstream epics exist or what they do | Investigation epic with conditional downstream epics. |\n228\t\n229\tWhen a strategy explicitly flags something as an open question, pending review, or conditional ADR, treat it as a genuine unknown — the strategy author has already classified it. Do not downgrade to an implementation detail based on descriptive text elsewhere in the strategy. A detailed description of current state is context, not a decision. If the strategy indicates the resolution could require a different approach (conditional ADRs, \"if X requires changes to Y\"), evaluate which downstream epics build on the current assumption and gate them on the resolution.\n230\t\n231\t## Step 7: Derive Acceptance Criteria\n232\t\n233\tEach epic gets acceptance criteria derived from:\n234\t- Strategy acceptance criteria allocated to this epic's scope\n235\t- HLRs mapped to this epic\n236\t- Implementation-specific requirements (build pipeline green, rollback plan, doc review, etc.)\n237\t- Rules 23-25 from Step 5\n238\t\n239\tEvery AC must be a testable pass/fail condition on THIS epic's own deliverable — something the epic's engineering work produces or verifies. Externally-controlled preconditions are not ACs, in either form: schedule constraints (turnaround you do not control — accredited-lab queues, review-board cadence, upstream vendor timing) or availability preconditions (procurement, dedicated hardware or node allocation, partner-lab access, environment provisioning) — anything granted by parties outside the strategy belongs in the epic's Risks/Notes or the summary's Health Warnings. Write the AC at the engineering completion point you do control — \"the evidence package is submitted to the certification lab and triaged\" is a valid AC; \"lab scheduling and review-board cadence are externally controlled and cannot be compressed\" is a schedule-risk note misfiled as an AC; \"dedicated hardware nodes are available to the campaign\" is an availability precondition misfiled as an AC — the epic's work may include *securing* access, but the access being granted is not a condition the epic's deliverable produces, so it stays in Risks/Notes while the AC sits on the deliverable itself (e.g. the campaign's validated report).\n240\t\n241\t## Step 8: Generate Artifacts\n242\t\n243\t### Step 8a: Write decomposition summary (the plan)\n244\t\n245\tWrite the decomposition summary **first** — this is the blueprint for all epic files.\n246\t\n247\tWrite `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md` in two steps:\n248\t\n249\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections:\n250\t   - **Epic List** (table: ID, title, type, team, priority)\n251\t   - **Dependency DAG** (Mermaid `graph TD` diagram — roots at top, arrows point from dependency to dependent: `E001 --> E003` means \"E001 must complete before E003 can start\")\n252\t   - **DAG Justification** (table: edge, rule, rationale)\n253\t   - **HLR Traceability Matrix** (HLR → epic mapping, confirming full coverage)\n254\t   - **Health Warnings** (priority inversions, scope traps — if any)\n255\t   - **Tiered Delivery** (if applicable — Tier 1 vs Tier 2 split)\n256\t\n257\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n258\t\n259\t```bash\n260\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md \\\n261\t    parent_strat=\"{ID}\" epic_count=<N> critical_path_length=<N>\n262\t```\n263\t\n264\tAdd `triage=<value> triage_rationale=\"<reason>\"` for triaged strategies (Step 0).\n265\t\n266\t### Scope constraint: decompose, don't design\n267\t\n268\tYour job is to break strategy scope into units of work, not to make implementation decisions.\n269\tIf the strategy describes a capability at a functional level, the epic scope stays at that level.\n270\tDo not invent API paths, URL schemas, response formats, environment variables, caching policies,\n271\tCRD field names, or other implementation details not stated in the strategy. Those are decisions\n272\tfor the implementing team.\n273\t\n274\t### Step 8b: Write per-epic files\n275\t\n276\tWrite one file per epic to `artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-ENNN.md` (e.g., `{ID}-E001.md`, `{ID}-E002.md`), following the decomposition summary as the plan. Each epic's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, and HLR mappings must match what the summary specifies.\n277\t\n278\tFor each epic, write in two steps:\n279\t\n280\t1. Write the body content (no frontmatter delimiters) with these sections (minimum — add additional sections when the strategy contains relevant content for this epic's scope, e.g., risks, assumptions, open questions, stakeholder commitments):\n281\t   - **Title** (one line)\n282\t   - **Description** (what this epic delivers)\n283\t   - **Scope** (specific changes in this epic)\n284\t   - **Acceptance Criteria** (derived from strategy)\n285\t   - **HLR Traceability** (which strategy HLRs this epic covers)\n286\t   The four section headings are literal and required for EVERY epic, including `docs-authoring` epics — an outline of content topics goes INSIDE the `## Scope` section, never as a renamed `## Content Outline` heading (a renamed heading fails the artifact contract).\n287\t   Signal rationales go in a separate file (see Step 6) — do not include them in the epic body.\n288\t\n289\t   **No cross-references to sibling epics.** Do not reference other epics by draft ID (e.g., \"E001\", \"E003\") anywhere in the body — not in descriptions, scope, acceptance criteria, or HLR traceability. Draft IDs are internal to the decomposition and meaningless once epics are created in Jira. Dependency relationships are captured by frontmatter `dependencies` and Jira Blocks links. Each epic body must be self-contained: describe what it delivers and depends on in plain terms (e.g., \"the OTEL env var injection capability\" not \"E003\") without naming sibling epics.\n290\t\n291\t2. Set frontmatter via script:\n292\t\n293\t```bash\n294\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n295\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n296\t    component=\"<canonical name from .context/rhai-components.txt>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n297\t    type=Implementation priority=P0 \\\n298\t    dependencies=\"{ID}-E002,{ID}-E003\" \\\n299\t    ai_signals.change_specificity=1 \\\n300\t    ai_signals.pattern_precedent=1 \\\n301\t    ai_signals.adapter_pattern=0 \\\n302\t    ai_signals.existing_foundation=1 \\\n303\t    ai_signals.open_questions=-1 \\\n304\t    ai_signals.external_dependency=0 \\\n305\t    ai_signals.human_process_gates=-1 \\\n306\t    ai_signals.repo_access=1 \\\n307\t    ai_signals.architecture_claims=1\n308\t```\n309\t\n310\tFor an **Investigation** epic, set `type=Investigation` and write the five\n311\t`investigation_signals` instead of `ai_signals` (do not set both):\n312\t\n313\t```bash\n314\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-E001.md \\\n315\t    epic_id=\"{ID}-E001\" title=\"<epic title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n316\t    component=\"<canonical name>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n317\t    type=Investigation priority=P0 \\\n318\t    investigation_signals.question_specificity=1 \\\n319\t    investigation_signals.source_accessibility=1 \\\n320\t    investigation_signals.local_runnability=1 \\\n321\t    investigation_signals.cluster_hardware_dependence=0 \\\n322\t    investigation_signals.human_judgment_required=0\n323\t```\n324\t\n325\tAdd optional fields only when non-null: `implementation_type=<value>`, `branch=<value>`, `gated_by=<epic_id>`, `gate_failure_impact.action=<value> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<text>\"`. Every epic that depends on an Investigation should have `gated_by` pointing to that Investigation (see Rule 3).\n326\t\n327\tDo **not** include `ai_implementability` or `ai_implementability_score` — the pipeline computes those from `ai_signals` (Implementation) or `investigation_signals` (Investigation) automatically.\n328\t\n329\t### Step 8c: Verify consistency\n330\t\n331\tAfter writing all epic files, run:\n332\t```\n333\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py batch-read artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-*E[0-9][0-9][0-9].md\n334\t```\n335\t\n336\tCompare the output against the decomposition summary. If any epic file's `dependencies`, `priority`, `type`, or HLR mappings diverged from the plan, fix the epic file to match the summary.\n337\t\n338\tThen run the contract validator until it passes:\n339\t\n340\t```bash\n341\tpython3 skills/epic-decompose/scripts/validate_decomposition.py {ID}\n342\t```\n343\t\n344\tIt deterministically checks what downstream consumers enforce and an LLM step can silently get wrong: epic body sections (Description / Scope / Acceptance Criteria / HLR Traceability), `component` values verbatim in `.context/rhai-components.txt`, Rule 11 (docs-authoring blocked by every Implementation epic), priority inheritance (an epic blocking P0 work is itself P0), and implementation-type parallelism (Rules 7/8/10 — no `dependencies` edge, in either direction, between `license-validation` and `repo-onboarding`, `license-validation` and `konflux-onboarding`, or `konflux-onboarding` and a general implementation; a flagged edge is removed from the dependent epic's `dependencies` and its coupling expressed as an AC gate instead). It prints one `VIOLATION:` line per problem and exits non-zero. Fix every violation by editing the epic files (never edit the script), re-run, and proceed only once it prints `OK`.\n345\t\n346\tThen, as your **final action** — after every epic file is written, any divergence is fixed, and the validator prints `OK` — mark the decomposition complete:\n347\t\n348\t```\n349\tpython3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-decomposition.md decompose_complete=true\n350\t```\n351\t\n352\tThe pipeline uses this field to detect that you have finished. Until it is set, the review agent is not launched. Do not set it earlier: anything you write or edit after setting it may be reviewed in a partially written state.\n353\t\n354\t### Conditional decomposition (when applicable)\n355\t\n356\tIf an Investigation epic has ≤3 bounded outcomes that change downstream structure, write one file per branch epic using the `-BRANCH-<letter>-` filename convention:\n357\t\n358\t```\n359\t{ID}-E001.md                        # Shared epic (the Investigation that selects the branch)\n360\t{ID}-BRANCH-A-E003.md               # If outcome A\n361\t{ID}-BRANCH-B-E003.md               # If outcome B\n362\t{ID}-BRANCH-B-E004.md               # Extra epic in branch B\n363\t```\n364\t\n365\t**Branch epics are not standalone Jira issues.** The pipeline attaches each branch's epics to the gating Investigation epic as a plan document; it does not create them as issues or wire Blocks links from them. Two rules follow, and both are enforced downstream — a branch file that breaks them is silently dropped:\n366\t\n367\t1. **Every branch file MUST set `branch` and `gated_by` in frontmatter** (in addition to the normal epic fields), plus `gate_failure_impact`:\n368\t   - `branch=<letter>` — the outcome label, matching the `-BRANCH-<letter>-` in the filename (`branch=A` for `{ID}-BRANCH-A-E003.md`).\n369\t   - `gated_by={ID}-E001` — the `epic_id` of the **main-plan Investigation** whose outcome selects this branch (must be a real main-plan epic). It **MUST also appear in this branch epic's `dependencies`** — `gated_by` is always a member of `dependencies` (the branch cannot start until the Investigation resolves).\n370\t   - `gate_failure_impact.action=<rewrite|remove|add_remediation> gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<text>\"`.\n371\t\n372\t   ```bash\n373\t   python3 scripts/frontmatter.py set artifacts/epic-tasks/{ID}-BRANCH-A-E003.md \\\n374\t       epic_id=\"{ID}-BRANCH-A-E003\" title=\"<title>\" parent_strat=\"{ID}\" \\\n375\t       component=\"<canonical name>\" team=\"<owner team>\" \\\n376\t       type=Implementation priority=P0 \\\n377\t       branch=A gated_by=\"{ID}-E001\" dependencies=\"{ID}-E001\" \\\n378\t       gate_failure_impact.action=rewrite \\\n379\t       gate_failure_impact.fallback_approach=\"<what changes if outcome A does not hold>\" \\\n380\t       ai_signals.change_specificity=1 ...\n381\t   ```\n382\t\n383\t2. **A main-plan epic MUST NOT list a branch epic in its `dependencies`.** Branch epics are not main-plan nodes, so a dependency on one (e.g. main-plan `E004` depending on `BRANCH-A-E003`) resolves to a nonexistent epic. Today these capabilities depend on an inline vector store provider bundled within the Llama Stack process; removing it (per RHAISTRAT-7474) will break them unless an alternative is available at the platform level.\n19\t\n20\t## Problem Statement\n21\t\n22\tGen AI Studio and Auto Rag currently rely on an inline Milvus provider embedded in the Llama Stack distribution image to store and retrieve vector embeddings. This inline provider runs inside the Llama Stack process itself.\n23\t\n24\tRHAISTRAT-7474 proposes removing inline providers from the Llama Stack distribution to improve GA readiness — shipping only what can be tested and maintained at scale, and aligning with Llama Stack's primary use case as a remote API server. However, no platform-level alternative exists today. If inline providers are removed without a replacement, any RHOAI user relying on Gen AI Studio's RAG capabilities or Auto Rag will lose functionality entirely — there is no workaround short of manually provisioning and configuring an external vector database.\n25\t\n26\tUsers expect vector storage to \"just work\" when they use Gen AI Studio or Auto Rag. The current out-of-the-box experience must be preserved even as the underlying architecture evolves.\n27\t\n28\t## Affected Customers\n29\t\n30\t* All RHOAI customers using Gen AI Studio playground with RAG capabilities\n31\t* All RHOAI customers using Auto Rag\n32\t* This is a platform-level product dependency: these features cannot function without a vector store\n33\t\n34\t## Business Justification\n35\t\n36\t* **Product integrity:** Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag are GA-track capabilities in RHOAI. Removing the inline vector store without a replacement breaks shipped product functionality for every user of these features.\n37\t* **Blocking dependency:** RHAISTRAT-7474 (removing inline providers for GA readiness) cannot proceed until this RFE is resolved. Silas Brenmark (Gen AI Studio lead) has identified this as a blocker.\n38\t* **User experience:** RHOAI differentiates on integrated, opinionated defaults. Requiring users to manually provision and configure a vector database before they can use the playground or Auto Rag degrades the out-of-the-box experience that customers expect from the platform.\n39\t\n40\t## Acceptance Criteria\n41\t\n42\t* \\[ \\] A default vector store is available out-of-the-box on RHOAI without requiring users to manually provision or configure external infrastructure\n43\t* \\[ \\] Gen AI Studio playground RAG workflows function with the default vector store with no loss of current capability\n44\t* \\[ \\] Auto Rag functions with the default vector store with no loss of current capability\n45\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store runs as a separate process, decoupled from the Llama Stack instance (not an inline provider)\n46\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store is scoped appropriately for multi-tenant environments (e.g., per-namespace isolation)\n47\t* \\[ \\] The default vector store is lightweight enough to run in resource-constrained environments without imposing significant overhead\n48\t\n49\t## Success Criteria\n50\t\n51\t* Users of Gen AI Studio and Auto Rag experience no functional regression when inline providers are removed from the Llama Stack distribution\n52\t* No additional manual setup steps are required for RAG workflows compared to the current experience\n53\t* RHAISTRAT-7474 is unblocked and can proceed to implementation\n54\t\n55\t## Open Questions\n56\t\n57\t* What is the preferred scoping model — per namespace, per Llama Stack instance, or both? (Silas noted per-namespace is preferred for isolation, but Auto Rag may need per-instance scoping)\n58\t* Should users have a migration path from the default vector store to a production-grade vector database? (Bram Sundqvist raised the importance of aligning with commonly-used vector DB providers for easier migration)\n59\t\n60\t## Strategy (AI Generated by Agentic SDLC Pipeline)\n61\t\n62\t> **Note:** The full strategy exceeds Jira's description size limit and is stored as an attachment: `RHAISTRAT-8004-strategy.md`.\n63\t\n64\t## Staff Engineer Input\n65\t\n66\t**Correction 1 — OGX does not auto-provision PostgreSQL.** OGX defaults to SQLite for storage (`storage.kv.type: sqlite`, `storage.sql.type: sqlite` in the OGXServer CRD). The odh-dashboard gen-ai BFF hardcodes SQLite when creating OGXServer instances for the playground (`kv_sqlite` and `sql_sqlite` in `llamastack_config.go`). PostgreSQL is a supported backend but must be user-configured with an explicit `connectionString` secret. The strategy's claim that \"every LlamaStackDistribution instance requires a PostgreSQL database\" is incorrect — introducing PostgreSQL is new work, not an extension of existing infrastructure.\n67\t\n68\t**Correction 2 — A Red Hat PostgreSQL image with pgvector already exists.** The `registry.redhat.io/rhel9/postgresql-16` image includes pgvector out of the box — confirmed in the [sclorg/postgresql-container Dockerfile](https://github.com/sclorg/postgresql-container/blob/master/16/Dockerfile.rhel9) (`INSTALL_PKGS=\"$INSTALL_PKGS pgvector\"`). PostgreSQL 18 (RHEL 9) also includes pgvector. Furthermore, the model-registry-operator already uses `postgresql-16` as its auto-provisioned database image, and `RELATED_IMAGE_POSTGRESQL_16_IMAGE` is already present in the rhods-operator CSV for disconnected installs. No custom image build is needed. No Konflux onboarding is needed. The 1-2 sprint image onboarding estimate in the strategy can be eliminated.\n69\t\n70\t**Architectural direction — platform-level database vs. self-provisioned.** Multiple RHOAI components now need PostgreSQL (model-registry, MLflow, and now OGX for pgvector). The preferred long-term direction is a platform-provided shared PostgreSQL managed via the DSC, where each component consumes a connection string rather than self-provisioning. A shared platform-provided PostgreSQL via DSC will not be available until RHOAI 3.6. For 3.5, Gen AI Studio must provision its own PostgreSQL instance.\n71\t\n72\t**Operator dependency for self-provisioning (RHAISTRAT-7164).** Self-provisioning PostgreSQL following the model-registry-operator pattern requires a RHOAI-controlled operator for Gen AI Studio. The ogx-k8s-operator is upstream and cannot carry RHOAI-specific provisioning logic. The dashboard operator modularization (RHAISTRAT-7164, In Progress) would provide this operator layer. This is a hard dependency — until RHAISTRAT-7164 delivers, there is no RHOAI-controlled operator where PostgreSQL lifecycle management can live. It will be challenging to commit this strategy to a specific release until that dependency is delivered.\n73\t\n74\t**Fallback if RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time.** If the dashboard modularization is not ready for 3.5, the fallback is to require customers to bring their own PostgreSQL for RAG capabilities in the Playground. Users would manually configure the OGXServer CR spec with their PostgreSQL connection details. This aligns with the breaking changes introduced in OGX 1.0, even though the Playground largely abstracts OGX from users. The development team should define a go/no-go gate for this decision as part of sprint planning.\n75\t\n76\t**Decouple from Auto Rag.** Auto Rag integration with Gen AI Studio (RHAISTRAT-7824) is targeting RHOAI 3.6. This strategy should validate pgvector only for Gen AI Studio Playground RAG workflows. Auto Rag compatibility with pgvector will be addressed in RHAISTRAT-7824's scope. Remove Auto Rag from affected components, impacted teams, acceptance criteria, and validation requirements.\n77\t\n78\t**Performance and index thresholds — dev experimentation scope.** The default pgvector instance is meant for development experimentation, not production usage. Strict latency SLAs (p50/p95/p99) are not required. The sprint 1 benchmark should capture the inline Milvus baseline and verify pgvector is in the same order of magnitude, not meet a specific threshold. Typical Playground RAG usage involves small document sets — flat scan (no index) is sufficient for the default. Users with production-scale vector workloads should use an external vector database. Remove open questions about latency thresholds, corpus size ranges, and index type selection.\n79\t\n80\t**PostgreSQL resource sizing.** Reference the model-registry-operator's PostgreSQL resource requests/limits as the starting point. Adjust based on sprint 1 benchmarking if needed.\n81\t\n82\t**Alternative fallback — BFF-managed PostgreSQL provisioning.** If RHAISTRAT-7164 does not land in time, an alternative to requiring customers to bring their own PostgreSQL is to have the gen-ai BFF provision the PostgreSQL/pgvector instance directly, similar to how the BFF currently provisions guardrails infrastructure. The BFF would create the PostgreSQL Deployment, Service, PVC, and Secret when a playground with RAG is configured, if one does not already exist in the namespace. Caveats: (1) the implementation must be designed for portability — when the platform-provided shared database becomes available (3.6), the BFF should consume the shared connection string rather than self-provisioning; (2) lifecycle management of the PostgreSQL instance must be carefully considered — the BFF is not an operator with a reconciliation loop, so cleanup on playground deletion, handling of pod restarts, and credential rotation need explicit design attention.\n83\t\n84\t**Existing remote vector store implementation is reusable.** Per the engineering team, the existing remote vector store implementation can be largely reused for pgvector integration. The majority of the work effort is around infrastructure and provisioning of the PostgreSQL/pgvector database, not the vector_io provider integration itself.\n85\t\n86\t**Correction 3 — Vector storage and application storage are independent configurations.** The OGX vector_io provider configuration (`remote::pgvector` via `ENABLE_PGVECTOR`) is completely separate from OGX's application storage backend configuration (`storage.kv.type`, `storage.sql.type`). This strategy only needs to configure the pgvector vector_io provider — it does not change the application storage backend, which remains on its existing default (SQLite). [source: Dockerfile.konflux:52, Dockerfile.konflux.dashboard-operator:37, dashboard-operator/charts/dashboard/values.yaml:18]\n15\t\n16\t**Detailed**: odh-dashboard is a multi-component platform console consisting of three tiers: (1) a React/PatternFly single-page application served via Webpack Module Federation that hosts domain-specific UI modules; (2) a Node.js Fastify backend that proxies Kubernetes API requests using user impersonation and serves static assets behind kube-rbac-proxy; and (3) a Go operator (dashboard-operator) built on controller-runtime v0.23.3 that reconciles Dashboard custom resources, managing the lifecycle of the console deployment including RBAC, routes, and sidecar BFF services. The federated architecture includes ten Go BFF (backend-for-frontend) sidecars — core-bff, gen-ai, model-registry, mlflow, eval-hub, maas, agent-ops, automl, autorag, and data-registry — each serving domain-specific API endpoints on dedicated TLS-encrypted ports with Bearer token authentication. The operator watches platform CRDs (DataScienceCluster, DSCInitialization, KServe InferenceService, ModelRegistry, MLflow, TrustyAI, Feast) to reflect platform state in the dashboard and manages Gateway API HTTPRoutes for request routing. A bundled Workspace controller reconciles kubeflow.org/v1beta1 Workspace and WorkspaceKind resources with validating and conversion webhooks. Each UI module is paired with a dedicated Go BFF sidecar that handles its backend operations, creating a vertically-sliced architecture where each domain owns its full request path from UI through BFF to Kubernetes API. The federation configuration (in `manifests/rhoai/base/federation-configmap.yaml`) maps path prefixes to sidecar ports, enabling a single ingress point to fan out to domain-specific backends. [source: manifests/rhoai/base/federation-configmap.yaml:15, backend/src/routes/module-federation.ts:1]\n21\t\n22\tThe dashboard-operator reconciles Dashboard custom resources created by the rhods-operator, deploying and configuring the console pod alongside its BFF sidecars. The operator implements a declarative ownership model where the parent Dashboard CR controls the lifecycle of Deployments, Services, Routes, NetworkPolicies, PodDisruptionBudgets, and RBAC resources via controller-runtime's `Owns()` watches. Controller watches on platform CRDs (DataScienceCluster, DSCInitialization, KServe InferenceService, ModelRegistry, MLflow, TrustyAI, Feast) enable the dashboard to reflect the real-time state of the AI platform without polling. The operator uses `odh-platform-utilities` for platform detection, manifest rendering, and deployment helpers. [source: dashboard-operator/charts/dashboard/values.yaml:15-18, dashboard-operator/go.mod:6, dashboard-operator/config/rbac/role.yaml:1]\n23\t\n24\tAuthentication follows a two-layer model: kube-rbac-proxy fronts the Node.js backend (port 8443) performing OpenShift OAuth validation and injecting identity headers (`x-forwarded-access-token`, `x-auth-request-user`, `x-auth-request-groups`), while each Go BFF sidecar independently validates Bearer tokens and performs SubjectAccessReviews against the Kubernetes API for fine-grained authorization. The agent-ops BFF extends this with per-agent RBAC via SubjectAccessReviews for agent-specific access control. The Node.js backend additionally proxies Kubernetes API calls (`/api/k8s/*`) by converting user tokens to impersonation headers, allowing the frontend to interact with the cluster API through the dashboard service boundary.
